prompt_text:
The figure compares how adult tissue regeneration and cancer are linked across several organs, highlighting shared cell-state programs. In skin, lung, muscle, intestine, heart, and liver, injury appears to trigger temporary activation of stem or progenitor-like behaviors such as self-renewal, de-differentiation, proliferation, and altered differentiation. These regenerative responses are paired with key signaling cues, including pathways such as TGFβ, EGFR, NOTCH, YAP/TAZ, WNT, and MYC, as well as mechanical forces and niche signals.

A central theme is that normal repair uses plasticity in a controlled way, but persistent or misregulated activation can shift toward tumor formation. In skin, basal and differentiating keratinocyte compartments are linked to basal cell and squamous cell carcinomas. In the lung, alveolar and airway cells show injury-induced plasticity that resembles routes toward abnormal growth. Muscle regeneration involving satellite cells and YAP/PKA signaling is connected to rhabdomyosarcoma. In the intestine, stem-cell renewal and blocked Paneth-cell differentiation are associated with hyperplasia and colorectal cancer. Heart regeneration is depicted through cardiomyocyte de-differentiation and proliferation. In the liver, loss of quiescence and lineage switching among hepatocytes and biliary cells are tied to hepatocellular carcinoma and cholangiocarcinoma.
